steps: Clean the fish thoroughly and pat it dry, then score the skin diagonally a few times on each side so the marinade can penetrate and the skin crisps evenly.
Blend the spice paste ingredients (turmeric, chili, garlic, ginger) into a smooth paste, adding a splash of oil if it needs loosening.
Rub the paste all over the fish, inside and out, working it into the scored cuts, then season generously with salt and pepper.
Cover and let the fish marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 2 hours in the fridge for deeper flavor.
Preheat the grill to medium-high heat and oil the grates well so the skin doesn't stick and tear.
Place the fish on the grill and cook for 6-8 minutes per side, basting with oil every couple of minutes.
Turn carefully once the skin releases easily from the grates -- the fish is done when the flesh flakes easily and the skin is charred in spots.
Rest for a few minutes off the heat, then serve with a wedge of lime.
Pat the goat chunks dry and season generously all over with salt and pepper, pressing the seasoning into the meat.
Let the seasoned meat sit at room temperature for 20-30 minutes so it cooks more evenly.
Rub the meat lightly with cooking oil to help it brown and keep it from sticking on the grill.
Preheat a charcoal grill until the coals are glowing with a light ash coating -- this slow, steady heat is what makes nyama choma tender.
Grill the goat over indirect heat, turning every few minutes, for about 40-45 minutes total.
Move the pieces closer to direct heat for the last few minutes to build a deep char on the outside.
Check for doneness by piercing a thick piece -- the juices should run clear and the meat should pull apart easily.
Rest briefly, then chop into bite-sized pieces and garnish with a generous handful of chopped fresh coriander before serving.
Bring the steaks to room temperature for about 20 minutes before cooking so they sear evenly.
Mince the garlic and rub it all over both sides of the steaks along with a generous seasoning of salt and pepper.
Drizzle with oil, working it into the meat, then cover and marinate for at least an hour -- longer develops more flavor.
Light the braai and let the coals burn down until they're covered in white ash and radiating steady heat.
Place the steaks over the hottest part of the fire and sear for 2-3 minutes per side without moving them, to build a good crust.
Move to slightly cooler coals and continue grilling to your preferred doneness, turning once more.
Use a meat thermometer or the touch test to check doneness -- about 54C for medium-rare.
Rest the steaks on a board for at least 5 minutes before slicing so the juices redistribute.
Whisk the spice blend together with the coconut milk and oil until well combined into a fragrant marinade.
Add the chicken pieces to the marinade and turn them to coat every surface evenly.
Cover and let the chicken marinate for at least 20 minutes, or up to a few hours in the fridge for deeper flavor.
Preheat the grill to medium heat -- too hot and the coconut milk marinade will scorch before the chicken cooks through.
Lift the chicken from the marinade, letting the excess drip off, and reserve the marinade for basting.
Grill the chicken pieces, turning every few minutes and basting with the reserved marinade each time you flip.
Continue grilling for about 20-25 minutes total, until the outside is golden and slightly charred.
Check that the chicken is cooked through -- juices run clear, no pink near the bone -- before serving hot.
Chop the tomatoes, onion, and chili finely, keeping them separate for now.
Season the fish lightly with salt and pat it dry so it sears rather than steams.
Heat a splash of oil in a wide pan and sear the fish pieces briefly on each side just to color the outside, then set aside.
In the same pan, saute the onion until soft and translucent.
Add the tomatoes and chili, and cook down, stirring occasionally, until the tomatoes break apart into a thick sauce.
Season the sauce with salt and a splash of water if it looks too thick, then let it simmer for a few minutes to meld the flavors.
Nestle the seared fish back into the sauce, spooning some sauce over the top.
Cover and simmer gently for 8-10 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily and the sauce has thickened to your liking.
Slice the onion and mince the garlic.
Heat oil in a heavy pot and saute the onion until soft, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant, about a minute.
Add the chicken pieces and brown them lightly on all sides, about 5 minutes -- this is about building flavor, not cooking through yet.
Season the chicken with salt as it browns.
Pour in the coconut milk, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low and cover.
Simmer for 30-35 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender and cooked through.
Uncover for the last 5-10 minutes if the sauce needs to thicken further, then taste and adjust the seasoning before serving.
Combine the jerk spice blend, scotch bonnet chili, and fresh thyme in a mortar or food processor and grind into a coarse, fragrant paste.
Stir the lime juice and oil into the paste until it forms a thick, spreadable marinade.
Score the chicken pieces lightly and rub the marinade all over, working it under the skin where you can for maximum flavor.
Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least an hour -- overnight develops the best, deepest flavor.
Bring the chicken to room temperature for 20-30 minutes before grilling.
Preheat the grill to medium heat and set it up for indirect cooking if possible, since jerk chicken benefits from a slower cook.
Grill the chicken, turning often to keep the sugars in the marinade from burning, for about 30-35 minutes total.
In the final few minutes, move the chicken over direct heat briefly to build a deep char on the skin.
Check that the chicken is cooked through before serving hot, ideally with extra lime wedges on the side.
Chop the tomatoes and onion, and mince the garlic.
Cut the fish into even chunks and season lightly with salt.
Heat oil in a pot and saute the onion until soft and golden, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Stir in the curry spice blend and cook for about a minute, until it darkens slightly and smells fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook down until they soften and start to break apart into a sauce.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring the sauce to a gentle simmer, stirring to combine everything smoothly.
Let the sauce simmer for 8-10 minutes to develop flavor before adding the fish.
Add the fish chunks, spooning sauce over them, and simmer gently for another 8-10 minutes until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily.
Taste and adjust the seasoning, then serve hot with rice.
Finely chop the onions -- the classic method cooks them low and slow in their own moisture before any oil is added.
Cook the onions in a dry pot over low heat, stirring often, for 20-30 minutes until deeply caramelized and jammy.
Stir the oil (or butter) into the softened onions.
Add the minced garlic and berbere spice blend, and cook for a minute or two until fragrant.
Add the chicken pieces and stir to coat them in the spiced onion mixture, browning lightly for a few minutes.
Pour in enough water to come partway up the chicken, then cover and bring to a gentle simmer.
Simmer for 40-45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is very tender and the sauce has thickened.
Nestle the hard-boiled eggs into the sauce, spooning some sauce over them so they soak up the flavor.
Simmer for a final 5-10 minutes to warm the eggs through, then taste and adjust the seasoning before serving.
Grind the spice paste ingredients together with the garlic and chili into a smooth, fragrant paste.
Season the beef cubes with salt and pepper.
Combine the beef, spice paste, and coconut milk in a pot and bring to a simmer.
Cover and simmer gently for 45-60 minutes, until the beef is fork-tender, stirring occasionally so the sauce doesn't catch on the bottom.
Once tender, lift the beef out with a slotted spoon and set aside, then continue simmering the sauce uncovered until it reduces and thickens.
Thread the beef cubes onto skewers, packing them fairly close together.
Preheat a grill or grill pan to medium-high heat.
Grill the skewers briefly, turning often and basting with the reduced sauce, until lightly charred -- this is mostly for color and aroma since the beef is already cooked.
Serve the skewers drizzled with any remaining sauce.
Combine the lime juice, sliced onions, oil, chili, salt, and pepper in a large bowl or bag.
Add the chicken pieces and turn to coat thoroughly in the marinade.
Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, turning occasionally -- the lime juice does most of the flavor work here.
Lift the chicken from the marinade, shaking off the excess, and set the marinated onions aside separately.
Grill or pan-fry the chicken over medium-high heat until browned on all sides, about 10-12 minutes -- it doesn't need to be fully cooked through yet.
In a separate pan, fry the reserved onions over medium heat, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 15 minutes.
Return the browned chicken to the pan with the onions and pour in the reserved marinade.
Cover and simmer gently for 20-25 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through and the onions have melted into a soft, tangy sauce.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with more salt or lime juice before serving.
Pat the goat chunks dry and season lightly with salt.
Heat oil in a heavy pot and fry the curry spice blend and minced garlic together for about a minute, until fragrant.
Add the goat and brown it on all sides, turning occasionally, for about 8-10 minutes.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes and cook for a few minutes until they start to soften and release their juices.
Add enough water to just cover the meat, then bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer gently for about 75-90 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the fresh thyme or curry leaves partway through cooking so their flavor infuses the sauce.
Check the goat for tenderness -- it should pull apart easily with a fork; if not, keep simmering, adding a little more water if needed.
Uncover for the last 10-15 minutes if the sauce needs to reduce and thicken, then serve hot.
